A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income

Donghoon Lee, Daniel Mangrum, Joelle W. Scally, Tejas Sinha, and Wilbert van der Klaauw

Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

This analysis accompanies the latest Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, by the New York Fed’s Center for Microeconomic Data. The report shows that total nominal household debt balances increased by $334 billion in the third quarter of 2026, a 1.8 percent increase from the second quarter of 2026. Although delinquency rates for mortgages worsened slightly, transition rates into serious delinquency were largely unchanged across non-housing debt types.

Note: The Quarterly Report and this analysis are based on the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, which is drawn from anonymized Equifax credit reports. 

A Widening Gap by Neighborhood Income

We begin our analysis by showing trends in the rate of newly delinquent credit card balances segmented by quartiles of average zip code income. These delinquency rates declined for all groups and converged during the pandemic, when forbearances, stimulus payments, and reduced consumption led to improved payment behavior. Since 2022, however, this measure of household distress worsened. Recent delinquency rates are higher than pre-pandemic levels for all groups, and the gap between borrowers living in higher-income neighborhoods and lower-income neighborhoods has expanded.

As previously noted, this surge partially represents a reversal of pandemic-era dynamics: federal economic stimulus compressed delinquency rates during the pandemic, but today, most households have exhausted their pandemic-era savings and most fiscal and monetary supports have ended. In addition, macroeconomic headwinds —namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs —have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets.  

Loosening Credit Standards During the Pandemic 

Although macroeconomic conditions were likely the main contributing factor to the reduction and subsequent increase in delinquency rates, we also explore whether the pandemic-era loosening in credit supply played a role. During the pandemic, deferments, forbearances, and loan modifications contributed to increasing credit scores because many borrowers who would have otherwise been reported past due avoided delinquency. Concurrently, strong consumer demand combined with low interest rates may have prompted some lenders to ease underwriting standards and extend credit to those previously not served.  

In the chart below, we plot the share of new credit cards (blue) and new credit limits (red) in each quarter extended to borrowers in the lowest quartile of neighborhood income (the same group comprising the blue line in the first chart). At the start of the pandemic, the share of new cards and credit limits going to these borrowers each rose by nearly 2 percentage points, and the shares remained elevated until 2023, consistent with lenders easing underwriting standards during that period.

Evidence from credit scores further confirms this easing. The chart below shows that the median credit score at card issuance fell from an average of 699 in 2017–19 (green region) to 688 during the 2020–22 period (red region). Notably, the decline in median credit score at origination likely understates the extent of easing since credit scores in the population were generally increasing during the same time, as shown in the blue line. However, this trend reverted toward the end of 2022, similar to the trend in card issuance to low-income areas, with median credit scores for new cards for more recent vintages surpassing the pre-pandemic (green) era. 

Pandemic-Era Credit Card Originations Had Lower Credit Scores

Source: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax.Note: Credit score is Equifax Risk Score 3.0.

Next, we explore how each of these vintages performed given their varied credit quality at issuance. The chart below decomposes our serious delinquency transition rate, the share of balances that became newly 90 or more days delinquent, by the same three vintages in the chart above along with the cards issued prior to 2017. Here we see a similar pattern across most vintages. Most new delinquencies in each quarter come from more recent vintages, as newly opened “unseasoned” debts have historically been the most likely to fall past due. The cards issued prior to 2017 had already reached their peak delinquency rate by 2018 and were waning in their contribution to the whole throughout the series.  

Meanwhile, the 2017-19 vintage reached its relatively low peak during the pandemic era where forbearances and fiscal and monetary supports helped produce historical lows in delinquency. On the other hand, the 2020-22 vintage showed a rapid rise and high peak throughout 2023 and into 2024 where it made up a sizable share of new delinquencies across all vintages, perhaps due to the relatively lower credit quality of this vintage. Notably, cards issued since early 2023 have generally gone to borrowers with higher scores. 

The Effect of the Pandemic-Era Vintage is Waning

Note: The value of each bin is calculated as the balance of loans originated in the corresponding 3-year vintage that is newly 90+ days delinquency in the current quarter divided by the total balance across all vintages that was not 90+ days delinquent in the previous quarter, annualized using a four-quarter moving sum.Source: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax.

What Does This Mean for Delinquency Rates Moving Forward? 

Delinquency rates for cards issued during the pandemic are abating. If current patterns hold, the elevated delinquencies of the past few years may prove to be more of a pandemic-era echo than a permanent feature of the credit card market—one that may continue to fade as 2020-22 vintages make up a shrinking (and positively selected) share of “surviving” cards.  

Of course, since newer cards are more likely to fall past due, the largest factor for near-term delinquency rates is the credit quality of the most recently issued cards. Thus far through 2025, the credit quality of new issuances, as captured by origination credit scores, is below that of 2024 but above the levels of the pre-pandemic and pandemic eras. So, absent macroeconomic shocks, we anticipate that new credit card delinquencies will likely continue to see signs of improvement, and we will continue to monitor the trends in card performance in the coming quarters.
